stem: While taking a Pap smear, which site must be sampled because it is the area most likely to be affected by dysplasia and cervical cancer?
explanation: Almost all CIN and cervical cancers arise in the transformation zone at the squamo-columnar junction, so the spatula and brush must sample this area (360 degrees around the external os).

stem: Which of the following is used to take a Pap smear?
explanation: The Ayre's spatula (with or without a cytobrush) is used to scrape cells from the transformation zone. A colposcope only magnifies the cervix.

stem: The commonest cause of cervical cancer and cervical dysplasia is:
explanation: High-risk HPV (mainly types 16 and 18) is found in over 99% of cervical cancers. Early intercourse, multiple partners, smoking and immunosuppression are only cofactors.

stem: Among the many genotypes of HPV, which are the most oncogenic types causing invasive cervical cancer?
explanation: HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers. Types 6 and 11 cause genital warts and are low risk.

stem: A vaccine is available for the prevention of cervical cancer. It is directed against which HPV type?
explanation: HPV vaccines target the high-risk types 16 and 18 (the 9-valent also covers 31, 33, 45, 52, 58). Type 16 is the most oncogenic of the listed options.
key_note: Some paper keys marked B (HPV 11); correct is C (HPV 16): type 11 is a low-risk wart type, 16 is the main oncogenic type covered.

stem: What is the best method to prevent cancer cervix in a young woman or girl (e.g. with a family history of cervical cancer)?
explanation: Primary prevention is by HPV vaccination before sexual exposure. Screening detects precancer but does not prevent infection.

stem: A 30-year-old woman requests HPV vaccination. You inform her that it is most appropriate for:

options.B: Only women with normal Pap smear can receive it
options.D: Only women with abnormal pap smear can receive it

explanation: Vaccination is most effective before sexual debut, so it is routinely offered to girls aged about 9-13 years; efficacy is poor once HPV exposure has occurred.

stem: Regarding the role of HPV testing in cervical screening, which statement is correct?

options.A: Its value lies in its extremely low negative predictive power
options.B: High risk HPV testing improves the sensitivity of cervical screening
options.C: HPV testing is carried out routinely on all cervical cytology specimen
options.D: HPV testing can be used as alternate colposcopy in high grade lesion
options.E: HPV negative women are referred for colposcopy

answer_text: High risk HPV testing improves the sensitivity of cervical screening
explanation: High-risk HPV testing is highly sensitive with a high negative predictive value, and is used for triage of low-grade cytology and test of cure. It does not replace colposcopy in high-grade lesions.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attends for annual examination and has been sexually active for 11 years. What is the most suitable screening method for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia?
explanation: Cervical cytology (Pap smear) is the screening test; colposcopy and biopsy are diagnostic and are reserved for abnormal results.

stem: Population-based cervical screening should be offered to which age group?
explanation: In the UK programme screening runs from 25 to 64 years (3-yearly to 49, then 5-yearly to 64).

stem: A 30-year-old woman had a normal cervical smear last month. How often should it be repeated until the age of 49 years?
explanation: UK programme: 3-yearly screening from 25 to 49 years, then 5-yearly from 50 to 64.

stem: A 30-year-old woman attends for annual examination, has no medical problems and uses barrier contraception. The Pap smear report is inadequate. What is the most suitable step?

options.E: Visual inspection of cervix with acetic acid

explanation: An inadequate sample cannot be interpreted, so the smear is simply repeated (after about 3 months to allow epithelial regeneration). Colposcopy is not indicated for an inadequate smear alone.

stem: Which of the following correctly correlates the grade of CIN with its histological features?

options.B: CIN 2 - Lower one-third involvement of epithelium
options.C: CIN 3 - Upper one-third involvement of epithelium
options.D: CIN 2 - Involvement of up to two-thirds of the epithelium
options.E: CIN 1 - Involvement of more than two-thirds of the epithelium

answer_text: CIN 2 - Involvement of up to two-thirds of the epithelium
explanation: CIN 1 involves the lower third of the epithelium, CIN 2 up to two-thirds, and CIN 3 the full thickness (carcinoma in situ).

stem: A 28-year-old woman has a Pap smear report showing CIN I. CIN type I is labelled when:

options.A: The deeper 1/3rd of epithelium is involved

answer_text: The deeper 1/3rd of epithelium is involved
explanation: CIN 1 means dysplasia confined to the lower (basal, deeper) third of the epithelium; CIN 2 involves two-thirds and CIN 3 the full thickness.
key_note: Paper keys marked B (superficial third/two-thirds); correct is A: CIN 1 involves only the deepest (basal) third of the epithelium.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has a Pap smear report showing CIN III. What is the risk of progression of CIN III to malignancy?
explanation: Untreated CIN 3 progresses to invasive cancer in roughly 20-30% over 10-20 years, so it must always be treated.
key_note: Figures vary by source (12-30%); 20% kept as marked in the papers.

stem: A 35-year-old patient has a Pap smear report showing mild dyskaryosis. What is the next step of management?
explanation: Mild dyskaryosis that is persistent or HPV positive is referred for colposcopy; this is the usual exam key.
key_note: One paper marked B (repeat smear after 6 months); colposcopy (A) is kept as marked by most papers and is current UK practice with HPV triage.

stem: A 35-year-old P3 woman has a cervical smear showing a low-grade lesion. How will you manage her?
explanation: A low-grade lesion is not treated on cytology alone; it is followed up with colposcopy or repeat cytology, not LLETZ, cone or trachelectomy.

stem: Pap smear shows LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion). What is the next step?
answer_text: Observation (repeat cytology/HPV testing; colposcopy if persistent), no immediate treatment
explanation: Most LSIL/CIN 1 regress spontaneously, so observation with repeat cytology or HPV testing (or colposcopy if persistent) is appropriate rather than treatment.
key_note: Options not available in the source; recall question.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has LSIL on Pap smear and colposcopy with biopsy confirms CIN 1. She wishes to preserve fertility. What is the best next step?
explanation: CIN 1 usually regresses, so conservative follow-up with repeat cytology is preferred; excision increases the risk of preterm birth in later pregnancies.

stem: A 45-year-old P4 woman presents with postcoital bleeding for 3 months. The cervix is hyperaemic and the Pap smear shows low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. What is the best management?
explanation: With symptoms (postcoital bleeding), colposcopy with directed biopsy is needed to exclude a higher-grade lesion or invasion before any treatment.

stem: A Pap smear report shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: HSIL needs colposcopic assessment with directed biopsy to confirm the grade and exclude invasion before treatment; hysterectomy and repeat smears are not appropriate.
key_note: Options C (colposcopy) and D (colposcopy directed biopsy) overlap; D kept as marked in the papers.

stem: A 38-year-old P4 had a cervical smear done for intermenstrual bleeding. It shows severe dyskaryosis. What is the next most appropriate step?
explanation: Severe dyskaryosis requires colposcopy; repeat cytology, HPV testing or routine recall are inappropriate.

stem: A 32-year-old P1+0 presents with postcoital bleeding for 3 months. Pap smear and biopsy report carcinoma in situ. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Carcinoma in situ (CIN 3) is treated by excision (LLETZ or cone) after colposcopic assessment of the lesion to exclude invasion; hysterectomy is over-treatment in a young woman.
key_note: Not marked in the source paper; answer by reviewer. No excision option is offered, so colposcopic assessment is the best choice.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with postcoital bleeding has a hyperaemic cervix. Her Pap smear shows high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia. What is the best management option?
explanation: Cytology alone does not justify treatment; colposcopy-guided biopsy confirms the lesion and excludes invasion before excision.
key_note: Source key marked E (LLETZ); see-and-treat LLETZ is acceptable in some protocols, but standard exam teaching is colposcopy-guided biopsy first, so D is given.

stem: A patient has a Pap smear showing CIN III and colposcopy is planned. You plan LLETZ at the same time. This treatment is appropriate in patients with:
explanation: LLETZ is suitable when the whole lesion is visible on colposcopy, well circumscribed and with no suspicion of invasion; invasive lesions need cone biopsy or radical treatment.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has colposcopy-directed biopsy showing CIN III. What is the best treatment?
explanation: CIN 3 is treated by excision of the transformation zone with LLETZ (large loop excision, also called LEEP), which also gives a histology specimen.
key_note: In one set LEEP and LLETZ are both listed and are the same procedure; LLETZ kept as marked.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has recurrent vaginal discharge for a year. Her Pap smear shows moderate to severe dyskaryosis. What is the best treatment option?
explanation: High-grade CIN is treated by LLETZ after colposcopic confirmation; hysterectomy is not first line for CIN.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with CIN III is to have LLETZ. What is the potential impact of the procedure on future pregnancy?

options.A: Increased risk of first trimester miscarriage
options.B: Increased risk of still birth in future pregnancy
options.C: Increased risk of second trimester miscarriage and preterm delivery
options.D: Increased risk of Caesarean section due to cervical dystocia

answer_text: Increased risk of second trimester miscarriage and preterm delivery
explanation: Excision removes cervical stroma, increasing the risk of second-trimester loss and preterm delivery (rising with the depth of the cone).
key_note: One paper marked a rearranged option (stillbirth and preterm delivery); correct is second trimester miscarriage and preterm delivery.

stem: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman has stage IA1 cervical carcinoma. What is the best fertility-preserving surgical option?
explanation: Stage IA1 without lymphovascular space invasion is treated by cone biopsy with clear margins, which preserves fertility (LLETZ excision is also used if margins are clear).

stem: A 32-year-old nulliparous woman is diagnosed with a 3 cm stage IB1 squamous carcinoma of the cervix. What fertility-sparing treatment would you recommend?

options.B: Large loop excision of transformation zone (LLETZ)
options.E: Radical trachelectomy with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy

answer_text: Radical trachelectomy with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy
explanation: Radical trachelectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy preserves the uterine body in IB1 disease, whereas cone or LLETZ is inadequate for a 3 cm lesion. Oophorectomy is not needed.

stem: A young woman's mother recently died of cervical carcinoma. The first symptom of cervical cancer is:
explanation: Early cervical cancer presents with abnormal bleeding (irregular, postcoital or intermenstrual); discharge and weight loss are later features.

stem: Choose the most common symptom of carcinoma cervix:
explanation: Postcoital bleeding is the classic and most common symptom of cervical cancer.

stem: The most common histological variety of carcinoma cervix is:
explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for about 80% of cervical cancers; adenocarcinoma is next.

stem: A 38-year-old otherwise healthy P5+0 smoker uses the combined oral contraceptive pill and presents with vaginal discharge and postcoital bleeding. Speculum examination shows an irregular cervix with a fungating growth on the anterior lip. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation: A visible cervical growth is biopsied directly for histological diagnosis; a Pap smear is a screening test and is unreliable for an obvious lesion.

stem: A 50-year-old P4+0 hukka smoker has postmenopausal bleeding for 4 months. There is a cauliflower-like growth on the cervix. What is the next step?
explanation: Examination under anaesthesia with biopsy gives the diagnosis and the clinical stage (with cystoscopy and proctoscopy if needed) for a visible cervical growth.

stem: A 39-year-old P6 woman presents with postcoital bleeding for three months. What should be your first investigation?
explanation: Speculum examination with cervical cytology is the first-line test for postcoital bleeding, followed by colposcopy and biopsy if abnormal.
key_note: Source key (Pap smear) kept per exam teaching.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has irregular bleeding for 6 months and a Pap smear suspicious for cancer. What will you advise?
explanation: A smear suspicious for invasion needs colposcopy with directed biopsy for histological diagnosis; repeat smear would delay diagnosis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a third marriage has postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding with weight loss for 6 months. Speculum examination shows cervical ectopy with rough surface that bleeds to touch. Which investigation will you perform to diagnose?
explanation: Colposcopy with Pap smear and directed biopsy evaluates a suspicious-looking ectopy to exclude carcinoma.
key_note: Source key kept; a cervical biopsy is the confirmatory test.

stem: A 45-year-old P4 has foul discharge and postcoital bleeding. Speculum examination shows a 3 x 4 cm fungating cervical growth; bimanual examination shows an 8-week-size uterus with restricted mobility. What is the most appropriate radiological investigation?
explanation: MRI is the best imaging for local extent (parametrial invasion, stromal depth, nodes) in cervical cancer; CT is poorer for soft-tissue spread.

stem: A 65-year-old P3 has a cervical biopsy showing invasion greater than 3 mm but not wider than 7 mm. According to FIGO, her stage is:
explanation: Invasion deeper than 3 mm and up to 5 mm with spread up to 7 mm is stage IA2.
key_note: One source had a student tick on A (Ia1); correct is B (Ia2).

stem: What is the FIGO stage of cervical carcinoma with microinvasion of the basement membrane less than 7 mm across, with no lymphovascular space invasion?
explanation: Microscopic invasion up to 3 mm deep and under 7 mm wide without LVSI is stage IA1.
key_note: Paper key marked B (Stage 3), which is clearly wrong; correct is D (Stage 1A1).

stem: A 40-year-old nulliparous woman has postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding. EUA shows a friable fungating 2 cm cervical mass; cystoscopy and rectovaginal examination are normal. What is the clinical stage?
explanation: A visible clinical lesion confined to the cervix and under 4 cm (2 cm here) is stage IB1.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has postcoital bleeding and a friable exophytic 4.5 cm cervical lesion; biopsy shows squamous carcinoma. What is the FIGO stage and best initial treatment?

options.A: Stage IB2 - Radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy
options.C: Stage IIA1 - Radical hysterectomy with lymphadenectomy
options.D: Stage IIB - Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery

answer_text: Stage IB2 - Radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy
explanation: A clinically visible lesion larger than 4 cm confined to the cervix is IB2 (2009 FIGO); the other options give the wrong stage for this lesion.
key_note: Under 2018 FIGO this lesion is IB3 and chemoradiation is preferred; A is the only option with a consistent stage and is kept as marked.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has cervical carcinoma extending beyond the cervix and involving the upper two-thirds of the vagina but not reaching the pelvic side walls. The stage is:
explanation: Upper two-thirds of the vagina without parametrial involvement is IIA; IIIA needs the lower third of the vagina.
key_note: One paper marked C (IIB); correct is B (IIA): IIB requires parametrial invasion.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding and a cervical growth extending to the vagina; biopsy shows squamous carcinoma. MRI shows extension to the lower one-third of the vagina with no parametrial invasion and no nodal involvement. What is the FIGO stage?
explanation: Involvement of the lower third of the vagina is stage IIIA; IIIB needs pelvic wall extension or hydronephrosis.

stem: A 45-year-old multiparous woman has postcoital bleeding and foul discharge for 2 months. A friable ulcerative cervical growth involves the cervix and upper vagina but not the pelvic wall. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingooophorectomy

explanation: Locally advanced disease beyond stage IB (here IIA bulky or IIB) is treated by concurrent cisplatin chemoradiation, not surgery.
key_note: Concurrent chemoradiation is the current standard; radiotherapy is the best option offered.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is diagnosed with cervical cancer infiltrating the parametrium. What is the optimal treatment?
explanation: Parametrial invasion is stage IIB and is treated by radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin; radical surgery is for stage IB to IIA.

stem: A 46-year-old P4 has irregular and postcoital bleeding. Examination shows a 6-7 cm cauliflower-like lesion replacing the cervix and involving the lower third of the vagina; histopathology shows squamous carcinoma. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Bulky, locally advanced disease (stage IIIA) is treated by concurrent chemoradiation.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is evaluated for carcinoma cervix and stage IV disease is found. What is the treatment?
explanation: Stage IV is not operable; stage IVA is treated with chemoradiation and IVB with palliative chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has biopsy-confirmed vulval cancer. What is the most common type of vulval cancer?
explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for about 90% of vulval cancers; melanoma and adenocarcinoma are rare.

stem: A 65-year-old woman has itching and a non-healing ulcer on the vulva for 4 months, with an ulcerative lesion on the right labium majus with raised irregular margins, induration and palpable inguinal nodes. What is the next step?

options.B: Excisional biopsy of the lesion and nodes
options.C: Wide local excision without lymph node assessment
options.E: FNAC of inguinal lymph nodes only

explanation: Histological diagnosis by punch biopsy of the lesion comes first; definitive surgery and groin management are planned after confirmation.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has pain and pruritus vulvae with a 2 cm ulcer on the left labium majus and palpable inguinal nodes; biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. What is the stage?
explanation: Spread to inguinofemoral nodes makes the disease stage III regardless of tumour size.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has a 1 x 1 cm firm left labium majus mass with ipsilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy; biopsy shows poorly differentiated squamous carcinoma confined to the vulva with no distant metastasis. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Treatment is radical local excision with inguinofemoral lymph node dissection (ipsilateral for a lateral lesion), with adjuvant radiotherapy if nodes are positive.
key_note: One source did not mark an answer; answer by reviewer.

stem: A 65-year-old woman has a 2 cm vulval growth with no stromal invasion and no palpable groin nodes. What is the treatment of choice?
explanation: Early small lesions are treated by radical wide local excision with 1 cm margins; radical vulvectomy is no longer routine.

stem: The most accurate method of assessing lymph node involvement in vulval cancer is:
explanation: Sentinel lymph node mapping and biopsy is the most accurate means of assessing groin nodes and avoids the morbidity of full dissection.
